newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Between films, German director stages operas.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Between films, German director stages operas.

text.p: Werner Herzog, the German film director, says directing an opera is a different kettle of fish.
For one thing, an interviewer suggested, you do not conceive your own projects. He nodded assent.
Or write the libretto. This point too was granted.

You are limited by the proscenium arch ("Yeah," he murmured, or perhaps "Ja"), by the demands of the music (obviously) and perhaps even by some diva's refusal to sing while turning her back on the audience.
Here a genuine chuckle escaped him. "I can handle that," he said. "I'm good at that."
He ought to be. The tall, long-faced 54-year-old with translucent blue eyes has spent three decades dragging cast and crew from jungle to desert to sheer rock peak.

For "Fitzcarraldo," his best-known film -- the fictional story of a rubber planter intent on bringing Caruso to the Amazon basin -- he provoked a fatal accident by winching a 320-tonne steamboat up a mountain. Then he sailed it down dangerous rapids, nearly causing a another disaster.
For the documentaries he churns out for European television, he has crawled to the lip of a smoking Caribbean volcano and crept to the foot of a blazing Kuwaiti oil well.
What, in fact, is such a strong-willed risk-taker doing amid the red plush of the Kennedy Centre Opera House?
"I never dreamt of being a director for opera," he said. "I was actually dragged into it by the hair."
His intense attention to the music in his films "was one of the reasons why people in the world of opera had a feeling of 'Yes, this is a man who should direct operas,'" he said.
Bologna got the feeling first. He staged two rareties there 11 years ago -- "Doctor Faustus," left uncompleted at Busoni's death, and "Giovanna d'Arco," an early Verdi considered unproducible.
"I always said if I do opera I want to take on challenges, unusual things, not, let's say, 'La Traviata,'" Herzog said.

He has been typically bold in his U.S. debut. With supertenor Placido Domingo in the title role, he is directing Carlos Gomes' "Il Guarany" ("The Guarani Indian"), a 19th-century hit since fallen into obscurity. It opened on Saturday for a seven-performance run that will end on Dec. 1.

"'Il Guarany' was composed for the La Scala opera house in Milan, and Verdi was the mentor of this young Brazilian composer, Gomes, and it became an instant and huge success, not only at La Scala but all over Europe," Herzog said. "It played for 30 consecutive years, until 1901, and then all of a sudden it was dropped out from all performances and all schedules and never played again, with only one exception -- for Brazilians it became some sort of a national opera."
He professes to find its general neglect inexplicable. "('Il Guarany' is) a real archaeological find and very, very exciting," he said. "... Some of it sounds like the very best of Italian opera."

He is honest enough to add that "the libretto, the story, is a total wild mess and disaster." Set in 16th-century Brazil, it involves a Spanish rascal, the irresistible daughter of a Portuguese grandee, one warlike and lecherous "savage" and one exceptionally noble one (Domingo).

But after a moment Herzog changed tack, calling the libretto "wonderful" and saying, "It has all the elements of a jungle delirium. It has all the elements of something that only occurs in fever dreams."

He has tried to bring out this hallucinatory quality in his production, a "more precise ... more complete and more spectacular" version of one he and many of the same principals collaborated on in Bonn two years ago.

For Domingo, a Spaniard who trained and began his career in Mexico, "Il Guarany" is a first step toward keeping a promise to highlight little-known Spanish and Latin American works. He made the vow before beginning this, his first season as artistic director of the 40-year-old Washington Opera.
For Herzog, it represents a chance "to live and breathe and work with music for three or four weeks, and that's very good, because it brings me back to my very balance."

"It is a wonderful privilege that I sometimes even abuse as a director that I can be in the middle of the music, standing just at arm's length from Placido Domingo," he reflected. "It's something that no one else has. Not even the conductor in the orchestra pit gets so close."
